transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I suppose I'm here because... well, it's my eating. Once I start eating those comfort foods, I tell myself, 'Maria, that is enough.' But my hand still goes back to the pot like I just can’t make myself stop. 

And it's a heavy pot, too! I got it at a rummage sale back in, oh, must be 1985. The lady selling it said it belonged to her grandmother. It’s cast iron, the kind you just don’t see anymore. They make everything out of that cheap aluminum now, and it warps the second it gets hot. My daughter bought a set last Christmas and she already had to throw half of it out. Such a waste of money, I told her, but young people just don't listen to you these days. They buy everything on that internet. 

Anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right. Yes, my hand just keeps going back for more food, even when I know I should stop.
When you find yourself eating past the point of fullness, do you feel like you’ve lost control over your eating during those moments?

Lost control? Well, I don't know if I'd call it that. I haven't really thought about it in those words, to be honest with you. It's more just... I'm sitting there, and the food is right in front of me. 

Like last Tuesday, I had made a whole tray of my sister's baked ziti. She gave me the recipe back in, oh, 1972 maybe? Right before she moved down to Florida. She moved down there for her arthritis, you know. The dampness up here just settled right into her knees, poor thing. She had that terrible doctor back then, Dr. Henderson, who never listened to a word she said. He kept telling her to just take aspirin. Can you imagine? Just aspirin for bones rubbing together! I always told her she needed to find someone else, but people were so loyal to their doctors back then. Anyway, she lives in Boca now. Or is it Tampa? No, Boca. It's very humid, but she says the heat helps her joints. 

...I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Something about the ziti?
When you're eating past the point of fullness, do you feel like you can't stop eating, even though you want to?

Yes, exactly! That's what I was trying to say earlier. I really do want to stop. I'll be sitting there and I'll tell myself, 'Maria, that is enough,' but my hand just keeps going right back to the pot like I can’t make myself stop. 

It's like my hand has a mind of its own. You know, speaking of hands, I was looking at my knuckles the other morning and thinking how much they look like my mother's did. She played the piano at the First Methodist Church every Sunday for forty years. They had this gorgeous old upright piano... mahogany, I think. Or maybe walnut? No, it was mahogany, because it matched the pews perfectly, and Reverend Thomas was very strict about things matching in the sanctuary. He was a wonderful preacher, though. He gave the most beautiful sermons. He passed away in... oh, it must have been 1992, bless his heart. His wife moved out West somewhere after the funeral. Arizona, maybe? 

But anyway... yes. Even though I know I'm full and I want to quit, I just can't seem to stop myself from taking more.
Has this difficulty stopping yourself from eating, even when you want to, caused you any distress or affected your daily life in any way?

Well, it does bother me, yes. I still go to Mass every Sunday, and I sing in the choir... oh, the choir! We are practicing for Easter right now, and let me tell you, Mrs. Higgins is trying to make us sing this new arrangement of 'Amazing Grace' that is just entirely too fast. It's supposed to be a hymn, not a race! I told her last Wednesday, I said, 'Martha, we are not trying to catch a train here.' But she has been so stubborn ever since she went to that choir directors' workshop in Chicago last fall. Chicago! I went there once in, oh, 1968 I think it was. The wind coming off that lake was something fierce. It ruined a brand new hat I had just bought at Woolworths. 

But, oh, what was I saying about my days? Right, my routine. I still take care of my home and everything, but... well, after one of those afternoons where I just can't stop eating, I get so terribly embarrassed with myself. I'll just stay in for the rest of the evening. I won't even answer the telephone if my friends call, because I just feel so ashamed of what I've done.
After you find yourself eating past the point of fullness, do you ever make yourself vomit, use laxatives, or do anything else to try to compensate for the food you ate?

Oh heavens, no! Make myself throw up? Never. I absolutely hate being sick to my stomach. And laxatives? No, I don't mess with those either. 

You know, my neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lived next door to us in the old house on Elm Street—she used to take those awful pink pills all the time. She swore by them. But she was a very nervous woman, always pacing around her yard pulling weeds. She had the most beautiful hydrangeas, though. Huge blue blooms! She told me the secret was putting rusty nails in the soil. Can you believe that? Rusty nails! My husband, Frank, tried it with our bushes, but they never turned out quite right. 

Frank did step on a rusty nail once, though, when we were building the back deck. This must have been... oh, 1984 maybe? We had to rush him to the emergency clinic over on 4th Street, and we ended up missing the entire neighborhood block party. It was such a shame, because I had made my famous potato salad. I use a little dash of paprika and sweet relish in mine, which is how my grandmother taught me to make it. She came over from Italy when she was just a little girl, you know. 

...But no, I don't do anything like that after I eat. Just the thought of making myself sick gives me the shivers.
Do you find yourself having episodes where you eat a significantly larger amount of food in a short period of time than most people would eat under similar circumstances?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. Some afternoons, especially after choir practice or if I've been out working in the garden... I have the most wonderful tomato plants this year, by the way. Better Boy tomatoes, they're called. I got the seeds from a catalog that came in the mail back in February. I usually order from Burpee, but this year I tried a new one, and oh, the tomatoes are just huge! I made a lovely tomato pie last week. Have you ever had tomato pie? You use a traditional pie crust, but then you layer the tomatoes with basil and a little mayonnaise and cheese... 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the food. Yes, so after choir or the garden, I'll fix myself a plate of something, maybe some rice and beans or a bit of chicken stew. But then... well, I just keep going back for more. I'll have another bowl, and then another, until I realize I've eaten enough for two or three full meals in just a sitting. It's terrible, really. But that tomato pie, I'll tell you, it's so hard to resist. I brought a slice to Mrs. Higgins, hoping it might sweeten her up a bit about that 'Amazing Grace' tempo, but she just thanked me and kept right on tapping her baton! Can you imagine?
When you find yourself eating much more than usual, does it tend to happen in a short period of time—like within a couple of hours—or does it happen more gradually throughout the day?

Oh, I really couldn't say for sure. I don't pay much attention to the clock when I get like that, you know? It just sort of happens. 

Speaking of clocks, though, we have this beautiful grandfather clock right in the front hallway. Frank bought it for our 25th wedding anniversary... oh, that would have been 1972, I suppose. It has the most lovely chime, Westminster chimes, just like the big clock in London! But it stopped working right around the time we had that awful ice storm a few winters back. Do you remember that storm? The roads were just a solid sheet of glass for three whole days. The mailman couldn't even get up our driveway, and he drives one of those sturdy little trucks with the chains on the tires. I had to have my nephew Tommy come over and put down salt on the front steps so I wouldn't break my neck trying to get the newspaper. Tommy is my sister's boy, the one who eventually moved down to Florida to open a bait shop. He says the humidity down there is just terrible for his asthma, but he loves being near the ocean. He sends me a box of oranges every Christmas. 

But anyway... what were you asking? Oh, the time. Yes, I just don't know. I'm not really watching the hours go by, so I couldn't give you an exact number. It just feels like once I start, the time sort of slips away from me.

Do these episodes of eating much more than usual happen in distinct periods where you feel like you can’t control your eating, or does it just kind of blend in with your regular eating throughout the day?

Well, it definitely feels like a distinct time, yes. Because once I start eating those comfort foods—like my famous macaroni and cheese, or that tomato pie I was telling you about—I just can't seem to stop. I'll tell myself, "Maria, that is enough," but my hand still goes right back to the pot. It’s like I can’t make myself stop, no matter what I say in my head. 

It reminds me of when my daughter, Susan, was little. She used to sneak into the cookie jar before dinner. I bought this beautiful ceramic jar shaped like a little cottage at a craft fair down in Springfield. Oh, the craft fairs they used to have! There was this one woman who made the most exquisite quilts. I bought a double-wedding-ring pattern quilt from her for my guest room. It has these lovely shades of peach and seafoam green. Anyway, I’d tell Susan, "No cookies before dinner," but she just couldn't help herself. She’d always leave a trail of crumbs right to her bedroom. She’s a lawyer now, you know. Up in Chicago. Very busy, always on the phone. She bought me a new tablet for my birthday so we could do those video calls, but I can never get the sound to work right. The picture is clear as day, but she always looks like a silent movie star! 

But yes, to answer your question, it doesn't just blend in. It's like a switch flips and I just lose all control of my hands and my mouth until I'm stuffed.

Do these episodes where you feel like you lose control over your eating happen in distinct, short periods of time—like within a few hours—or do they last much longer, such as over the course of an entire day?

Well, like I was saying before, it's usually just in the afternoon. You know, I come in from the garden or after choir practice, and I'll dish up some rice and beans or a bit of that chicken stew. And then I just keep going back for more, over and over, until I've eaten what would normally be two or three full meals. So it's all right then, in that one sitting. 

Speaking of chicken stew, my mother used to make the most wonderful stew. She would use the whole chicken, bone and all, and let it simmer on the stove for hours. The house would smell heavenly! We had this old gas stove, one of those big white enamel ones with the heavy grates. My brother, Charlie, he was always trying to sneak a taste before it was ready. Charlie was a rascal. He joined the Navy right out of high school, you know. Traveled all over the world. He brought me back a beautiful silk scarf from Japan once. It was a deep ruby red with little gold cranes embroidered on it. I still have it tucked away in my cedar chest upstairs. I don't wear it much anymore, it feels too fancy for just going to the grocery store or the pharmacy. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yes, it's just in that one sitting, not all day long. Just those afternoons where I keep going back to the pot until I've eaten two or three meals' worth.
Do you usually eat these larger amounts of food when you're alone, or do you often eat this way in front of others?

Well, I... I suppose I try to make sure nobody's around. I don't really want anyone watching me eat like that. It's embarrassing, you know? So I usually wait until I'm by myself in the house. 

My husband, Frank, he used to be home a lot more before he started volunteering at the VFW hall down on Elm Street. He's down there three afternoons a week now, helping them organize their bingo nights. They use those old-fashioned wooden balls with the numbers painted on them, not the electronic boards like they have over at the big casino. I went with him once, but it was so smoky in there, and the caller—a fellow named Arthur, who used to run the hardware store before it closed down—he talks so fast I couldn't keep up with my cards. Arthur's wife makes the most divine lemon pound cake, though. She brought one to the church bake sale last Easter, and it sold out in ten minutes flat. I managed to get a slice, and it had this glaze on top that just melted in your mouth. I asked her for the recipe, but she said it's a family secret passed down from her grandmother in Savannah. 

But anyway, yes, to answer your question... I definitely prefer to be alone when I eat like that. I wouldn't want Frank or anyone else seeing me go through three helpings of stew.

We had this old gas stove, one of those big white enamel ones with the heavy grates. My brother, Charlie, he was always trying to sneak a taste before it was ready. Charlie was a rascal. He joined the Navy right out of high school, you know. Traveled all over the world. He brought me back a beautiful silk scarf from Japan once. It was a deep ruby red with little gold cranes embroidered on it. I still have it tucked away in my cedar chest upstairs. I don't wear it much anymore, it feels too fancy for just going to the grocery store or the pharmacy. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. Yes, it's just in that one sitting, not all day long. Just those afternoons where I keep going back to the pot until I've eaten two or three meals' worth.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's episodes of overeating occur specifically in secrecy, which is a distinguishing feature of Bulimia Nervosa (F50.0) compared to Binge Eating Disorder (F50.81).
doctor.question: Do you usually eat these larger amounts of food when you're alone, or do you often eat this way in front of others?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I eat alone because of embarrassment about the amount I eat, which corresponds to a specific binge-eating symptom (eating alone) that is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I... I suppose I try to make sure nobody's around. I don't really want anyone watching me eat like that. It's embarrassing, you know? So I usually wait until I'm by myself in the house. 

My husband, Frank, he used to be home a lot more before he started volunteering at the VFW hall down on Elm Street. He's down there three afternoons a week now, helping them organize their bingo nights. They use those old-fashioned wooden balls with the numbers painted on them, not the electronic boards like they have over at the big casino. I went with him once, but it was so smoky in there, and the caller—a fellow named Arthur, who used to run the hardware store before it closed down—he talks so fast I couldn't keep up with my cards. Arthur's wife makes the most divine lemon pound cake, though. She brought one to the church bake sale last Easter, and it sold out in ten minutes flat. I managed to get a slice, and it had this glaze on top that just melted in your mouth. I asked her for the recipe, but she said it's a family secret passed down from her grandmother in Savannah. 

But anyway, yes, to answer your question... I definitely prefer to be alone when I eat like that. I wouldn't want Frank or anyone else seeing me go through three helpings of stew.
